transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees (as recorded): Jordan, Maya, Leo, Samir (Redwood); Alex, Priya, Tom, Eleanor, Marta (Sentinel)
Notes: technical deep dive focused on moderation placement, runtime overhead, KV cache/batching/quantization effects, and tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments (VPC/on-prem).

00:00 Jordan: Okay everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes. Quick intros, then Maya will take us through the latency-cost tradeoffs for different moderation placements.
00:13 Alex: Hi, Alex from Sentinel. We're mostly interested in real-time triage of clinical notes, so low single-digit hundred-millisecond latency for user flows is important.
00:21 Priya: Priya here, I run the ML infra team. We also have strict PII rules, so any inline moderation that touches raw text needs to be auditable.
00:30 Maya: Great context. Quick agenda: 1) where to put filters (inline pre, inline post, async), 2) how KV cache and batching change things, 3) quantization and model-compat implications on safety models, 4) VPC/on-prem constraints and fallbacks.
01:02 Tom: And I'll add security questions as they pop up — encryption/KMS, audit logs.
01:10 Maya: Cool. So first, placement basics. Inline pre-filter: run a lightweight classifier before calling the main LLM; pros: you avoid cost and KV cache churn for flagged inputs; cons: it's another model in the critical path that adds latency. We typically see a small lightweight transformer or even a heuristics layer.
01:45 Priya: Could you quantify "small"? 10ms, 50ms?
01:49 Maya: For a distilled binary classifier on CPU you might be 10-40ms depending on sequence length. On a CPU on private infra it could be slower. On GPU with a tiny model it's more like 5-15ms. But that's optimistic; cold starts and serialization add overhead.
02:10 Leo: And remember, that per-request overhead interacts with batching. If you can batch the pre-filter, you get amortized cost, but you also add latency for batching windows.
02:24 Jordan: Right — so one pattern is hybrid: pre-filter lightweight inline, then async heavier checks post-response for high-confidence negatives. That reduces false negatives exposed to users but keeps user latency low.
02:38 Alex: For clinical triage the tolerance for false negatives is low — we don't want anything risky getting through. But we also can't block critical workflows with long waits.
02:52 Maya: Exactly. Next, KV cache impact. If you place the safety filter before the main model call, you avoid warming the KV cache for inputs that will be dropped. That saves compute and lowers cost. But if the pre-filter is too conservative and sends fewer tokens to the main model, cache hit rates can be lower for conversation flows because fewer prefixes are seen.
03:18 Priya: Can you expand on that? I thought higher cache hit rate always followed more repeated prefixes.
03:22 Maya: Yes, if users have repeated prefixes the KV cache warms. But imagine you pre-filter and drop a bunch of near-duplicate noisy inputs — then the main model doesn't see those prefixes, which might reduce cache utility for subsequent related queries. There's a balance.
03:38 Samir: Also consider batching: if you pre-filter synchronously you might break batching windows for downstream model calls because each request now has an extra step. That can reduce throughput.
03:52 Maya: Exactly. In Redwood's hosted infra we can route pre-filter and main calls to different hardware pools — pre-filter CPU/GPU and main model GPU quantized. On private deployments you may have constrained hardware so you may prefer async post-filtering to simplify hardware needs.
04:15 Tom: How much does post-filtering hurt from a safety standpoint? If you do post-filter async you could produce a response and then later detect a violation — what's the recommended UX for that?
04:27 Maya: There are a few patterns: 1) Do post-filter and redact or retract responses (UX complexity), 2) Block downstream actions (like storage/forwarding) until post-filter completes, 3) Use a conservative pre-filter to reduce the chance of toxic content reaching users and rely on post-filter for audits.
04:44 Alex: Retracting content in a clinical app is risky. We generally prefer blocking user-visible content until checks pass.
04:50 Jordan: That pushes toward inline checks, but as discussed that increases latency and cost.
05:00 Priya: On cost: do you have numbers showing per-10k requests how much compute difference we see between inline pre-filter vs only post-filter?
05:08 Maya: Ballpark: with pre-filter inline (lightweight model) you might add 10-20% CPU/GPU cost but save 20-40% token cost because many calls to the main model are avoided. If your main model is expensive (many tokens or large context) savings can be material. If main model is small or calls are short, overhead may outweigh gains. We'll share micro-benchmarks after this call.
05:40 Leo: Important nuance: quantization choices on the main model can affect safety model parity. If the safety classifier was trained on float32 behavior and you run main model in int8 quantized variant, some emergent behaviors change. Not common for simple blockers, but for subtle hallucination checks it's relevant.
06:05 Maya: Right; we advise evaluating safety models on the exact serving configuration — same quantization and compiler flags. Compilers can fold operations that change tokenization or logits thresholds slightly.
06:18 Priya: Does Redwood provide guidance or tooling for running the same evals on quantized serving builds?
06:22 Samir: We do. We have a small harness to run prompt sets locally or in your private deployment; Maya will link the repo. It reports differences in classification thresholds, precision/recall drops, and where to tune.
06:35 Maya: I'll attach a demo recording. Next topic: batching mechanics and moderation. If you batch safety checks it reduces per-request overhead greatly, but increases tail latency due to wait-for-batch windows. For interactive flows where median latency matters, small batching windows (e.g., 5-10ms) help. For throughput-first paths, batch windows of 50-100ms are acceptable.
07:02 Jordan: Customers often ask: can we reuse safety outputs across similar inputs? Like hash inputs, cache safety decisions?
07:08 Maya: Yes — caching safety verdicts is a common optimization. We maintain a small LRU cache keyed on normalized text or a hash of the prompt. But cache staleness and rule changes are a risk. You need TTLs and invalidation on policy updates. Audit logs should record whether a cached verdict was used.
07:27 Tom: For compliance I'd want full auditable trail: original text, verdict source (model vs cache), model version, and KMS-wrapped logs.
07:36 Leo: Redwood's Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS and log retention in-region. We'll bring docs.
07:42 Alex: About KV cache and conversations: how do moderation decisions interact with KV cache tokens for few-shot prompts?
07:49 Maya: Good question. If you have an LLM chat session whose prefix includes system messages and user history, KV cache warmup depends on the exact prefix tokens seen. If moderation filters remove or rewrite a message, the prefix changes and KV cache hits for future messages may be lower. We sometimes maintain a sanitized prefix and an original prefix; the sanitized prefix is used for caching and the original for storage/audit, but that requires careful handling to avoid leaking content differences.
08:24 Priya: That sounds complex. Is it common?
08:27 Maya: It's common in regulated apps. The sanitized prefix approach means the runtime stores two versions and only exposes the sanitized to models. Again, storage/audit policies must be clear.
08:36 Alex: On deployment modes: if we run Redwood Private on-prem, what's the recommended pattern for safety filters? Inline or offloaded?
08:43 Maya: On-prem often favors inline but with lighter models due to limited GPU. Another pattern: host pre-filter on CPU nodes within the VPC and route main model to any available accelerator; for strict PII, customers like having both services inside the VPC so nothing leaves the network.
08:59 Tom: In that VPC pattern, do you support mutual TLS between components and audit logs at the edge?
09:04 Leo: Yes — mTLS between components, and all request/response metadata can be logged to your chosen storage. KMS/HSM integrations available for key rotation. We'll send the security pack.
09:12 Maya: Now some numbers on overhead. These are approximations from our internal tests: lightweight pre-filter (distil model) on CPU: 20-60ms median, 80-120ms P95. On a small GPU it might be 8-20ms median, 30-60ms P95. Main model call with 1k token context, small generation: median 120-220ms on optimized GPU quantized path, P95 400-700ms depending on load and batching.
09:56 Priya: So chaining them inline could push P95 above our tolerance. Any mitigations?
10:01 Maya: Yes — two engineering levers: 1) Asynchronous pre-filter with conservative short-circuit for high-risk tokens, 2) Smart routing: route premium customer flows to dedicated pools with tighter latency SLOs, 3) Dynamic batching windows and per-route batch sizing. Also pre-warm KV caches for known heavy prefixes.
10:22 Jordan: We also offer canary routes where a small percent of traffic goes through full synchronous checks to validate policies, and the rest goes through optimized path with conservative pre-filters.
10:34 Alex: How do we measure the moderation overhead in our SLA reports?
10:38 Leo: We emit per-request telemetry: total latency, time spent in each stage (pre-filter, main inference, post-filter), tokens generated, cache hit/miss. That shows up in Redwood Console per-route breakdowns.
10:49 Priya: Let's talk about quantization and classifier parity more — you mentioned differences. How big are the differences typically?
10:56 Maya: For simple binary toxicity checks it's often small (<2-3% delta in recall) when using 8-bit quantization on main model. For semantic safety checks that depend on nuanced logits ordering, deltas can be larger, maybe 5-10% depending on the model family. We recommend re-calibrating thresholds when switching quantization.
11:22 Tom: Does running safety models in FP32 and main model in int8 cause any coordination issues?
11:27 Maya: Not directly, but you might get disconnects in confidence calibration. So store model version and quantization metadata alongside verdicts so you can trace decisions back.
11:38 Alex: For high-volume bursts, caching seems key. Any advice on TTLs and sizing for cache of safety decisions?
11:45 Maya: TTL depends on policy churn; many customers use 24-hour TTL for user-submitted content, but for sensitive rules you might set shorter TTLs. Size depends on qps and diversity of input; we recommend sampling before sizing. We'll share a sizing spreadsheet.
11:59 Priya: If we go with dedicated capacity, does Redwood handle bursting to hosted if we hit our capacity?
12:05 Jordan: Yes, we support overflow/fallback policies. You can configure a graceful fallback to smaller cheaper model variants hosted by Redwood with reduced latency guarantees — with or without sending raw text off-prem depending on your privacy choice.
12:21 Tom: That off-prem option worries security. Do you have an option to only fallback to another private pool or deny?
12:27 Jordan: Yes — fallback policy can be strict: fail closed, redirect to private pool, or fail open with logging. We'll document the policy matrix for you.
12:36 Maya: Another interesting point: you can do model cascades — small classifier, then a specialist safety model, then the main model. Cascades reduce average cost but add operational complexity.
12:49 Alex: Is there a recommended cascade depth?
12:51 Maya: Two stages (light pre-filter + single specialist) is common. Three stages adds complexity; evaluate only if you have high qps and need very fine-grained precision/recall.
13:03 Priya: Let's get into concrete micro-bench numbers for our expected load: our baseline is 600 rps peak, average token generation per request ~150 tokens. Any back-of-envelope savings numbers?
13:14 Maya: Rough quick: main model cost is proportional to tokens * model cost. If pre-filter drops 20% of requests and those would have produced the same avg tokens, you save ~20% token cost. But pre-filter costs (assume 10ms CPU per request) scale with rps so you pay that across all. For 600 rps even 10ms CPU equates to significant CPU load; batching reduces that. We'll prepare a modeled spreadsheet with your numbers.
13:43 Jordan: We should run a small PoC: 1) run our microbench with your sample dataset, 2) evaluate pre-filter recall/precision, 3) simulate batching windows and KV cache warmup. Maya can run step 1 and Priya will share dataset.
13:56 Priya: We'll share a scrubbed sample and expected false positive tolerance.
14:01 Maya: Thanks. A few transcription quirks note: sometimes Fireflies mislabels speakers; ignore small attribution mismatches.
14:10 Jordan: Quick security note: for audit we recommend logging the model version, quantization, and routing decision on every moderation verdict entry. That helps if a third-party audit is requested.
14:23 Tom: Good. For encryption, does Redwood support in-transit and at-rest encryption with customer keys?
14:29 Leo: Yes, both. Private deployment allows BYOK and HSM integration. Hosted supports KMS and key rotation.
14:36 Alex: Regarding toolchain: we'd like to run canaries ourselves. Is there a sandbox API?
14:41 Jordan: We provide sandbox endpoints and a Canary config to mirror production routing. We'll include instructions.
14:47 Priya: A potential gotcha: how do we avoid double-charging for tokens if we run safety models and main models on the same input?
14:52 Maya: Billing vs cost distinction: Redwood billing usually charges for main model tokens; safety models can be billed separately depending on route. Internally, to avoid double cost, you can run caching of safety results or use lightweight heuristics to triage. We'll send detailed billing examples.
15:07 Marta: On the topic of false positives: what's the recommended UX when an input is blocked? Show an explanation or generic message?
15:15 Maya: Depends on compliance. For clinical apps you might show a specific remediation step (contact support, edit content) and log the rationale. Avoid exposing model internals.
15:24 Priya: For our audit needs we need retention of the original text for 90 days but only accessible to compliance team. Is that supported?
15:30 Leo: Yes — we can support role-based access and retention policies per-account in Private deployments. Hosted can also support longer retention as an add-on.
15:38 Jordan: Circling back, action plan: Redwood to run microbench, Maya to demo KV cache behavior with and without pre-filter, customer to send datasets. We will schedule a follow-up in two weeks.
15:52 Alex: Quick question — when you measured P95 for pre-filter, were those cold starts included?
15:57 Maya: Some of our numbers include steady-state only; cold starts add additional overhead. We'll include cold-start scenarios in the microbench report.
16:07 Priya: Any final notes on quantization: do you recommend int8 or int4 for main model in our use case? Long-term latency priority suggests int8. Int4 is risky for parity with safety checks and for hallucination sensitivity.
16:21 Maya: Agreed — int8 is a good starting point. Re-evaluate with your eval suite before moving to int4 or 4-bit formats.
16:30 Tom: Thanks, this was helpful.
16:33 Jordan: Thank you all. We'll send the deck, benchmark sheet, and security pack by next week. Follow-up scheduled: 2025-06-26.

Transcript end.
